paragraphs.text: Sacred teachings are a great provision for the soul on its way to salvation. Iron sharpens iron, and the divine word hones the soul. The body is fed by bread, but the soul is strengthened by the divine word. So the blessed Moses, pointing to the nourishing power of divine teaching, says: "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes out of the mouth of God." The word of God, then, is the food of the soul. The soul was made in the image of the Word who made the world, honored with reason and granted the freedom of a rational being. What could suit it better than a word that feeds it, trains it, and quickly brings it back to its own proper dignity? But by "word," brothers, we do not mean speech dressed up with a sophist's cleverness to make it persuasive. We mean the word whose truth is attested by the simplicity of faith. Every excellence of life and of speech that did not receive its first beginnings from the divine Teacher must be counted spurious. As far as a shadow is from the body, and a dream from the truth, so far does the reputed wisdom of the world stand apart from the true wisdom of God. That is why the blessed Paul, the chosen vessel, said what he did. He once set out wickedly to hunt down the saints, but was himself happily caught for the salvation of mankind. Expressly setting the pious and true word against the spurious one, he said: "Yet among the mature we do speak wisdom, though not the wisdom of this age, but the wisdom of God in a mystery." For us, then, wisdom is the tongue of the prophets, the teaching of the apostles, and the gospel of the kingdom, the summit of all authority in speech. And when we hear the word "gospel," brothers, let us give it a meaning worthy of the name. Many people, grown used to names through habit, have often failed to grasp the force of the things themselves. The gospel tells us what the reality is. It brings us the good news of the Savior's much-praised dispensation: that God came among human beings out of his love for mankind, not laying aside the dignity he had before the ages, but putting on the dispensation of salvation. The gospel brings us the good news that a physician has come to visit the sick, healing them not with drugs but by a mere nod of his love for mankind. It brings us the good news that a way has been shown to those who had strayed, that light has shone on those in darkness, and salvation on those who had been given up for lost. We had been trained by the law and did not turn back. We had been guided by prophecies and were not called back to the knowledge of the truth. There was danger that through our ingratitude everything would be ruined and human life would come undone. When God's love for mankind saw that we had given up under the training of the law and faltered under the guidance of the prophets, it overcame our ingratitude with great and measureless goodness. It set out the gospel of the kingdom for the whole world like a royal gift, and out of love for mankind it freely gave everything to the unworthy. So saving grace went forth and did good to all in various ways. It freed slaves, enriched the poor, recalled exiles and ransomed captives. It became all things to all, not because of our worth, but because of the goodness that befits the Benefactor himself. He is simple in nature, indivisible and without form, himself God from God, "the image of the invisible," "the radiance of glory and the imprint of the substance." Yet he takes on various titles, which do not fit his nature but suit his acts of kindness. Since everything human had fallen to ruin, he takes everything up into himself by making it his own, and he accepts these titles through the grace that renews all things. There was a great famine, a famine of the divine word. It was the famine God had threatened against the synagogue when he said: "I will send on them not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord."

He knew that the world was hungry and wasting away with famine, for what lack of food is to the body, lack of instruction is to the soul. So the fountain of all good things cries out through the Gospels: "I am the bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world." Bread for the senses comes from the earth, as it is said, "to bring forth bread from the earth." But the heavenly bread springs from heaven: "For I am the bread that came down from heaven." The earth was a desert, thirsty and deprived of the divine word, with no share in spiritual watering. What then? The same grace cries out again, pouring out its kindness like a spring: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink." The prophets had cried out in many ways, and the whole choir of the saints thirsted for his coming, saying: "O God, my God, I rise early to seek you; my soul has thirsted for the living God." Wishing to show that he is the one the prophets thirsted for, he cries out through the Gospels: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink." If anyone is like the one who said, "My soul has thirsted for you," let him come to me. Again, he saw the world naked. It was not naked in body but stripped of virtue. He saw the creature he had formed and had pity on what he had made, and to the naked he gives himself as clothing. As we said earlier on that occasion: "As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ." The earth had gone astray, seeking a way and not finding it. Every soul has within it the seed of the knowledge of God, but though it had this seed, it did not know how to hunt down what it longed for. Since those who had strayed could not find the way, he says: "I am the way." But are you dead? "I am the resurrection." But are you weak and in need of someone to lead you by the hand? "I am the rod from the root of Jesse," the rod that supports the weak. Of it the prophet said: "Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me." Why a rod, and why a staff? Because it suits every age: it disciplines the young and supports the old. "But, O Master, I was hungry and you fed me, thirsty and you gave me drink, naked and you clothed me. I had strayed and you guided me, I was weak and you gave me a staff. I have reached the road and found the footprints of piety. Now I seek the door of truth. Who will show it to me?" "I am the door; through me everyone enters to the Father." "Through you? Why?" "Because I am the open gate of salvation." This is the gate the blessed David seeks: he imagined many gates but found one. At first he says: "Open to me the gates of righteousness; I will enter through them and give thanks to the Lord." But he obtained his request and found what he had not expected, not many gates but one. Then he took back his own words and said: "This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it." Then, by prophetic vision and the longing of his soul, he passed within, and as if he were already inside the palace he says: "I will give thanks to you, for you have heard me." Tell us, prophet and theologian: you confess and give thanks to God, but what did you find that was worthy of your expectation? People who long to enter a royal residence expect to feast their eyes on what they will see there: much gold, gleaming marble, the many-colored flowers of wealth, the guard around the king, the royal throne, the gifts of kings. Each one expects to see these things, thirsts for the palace, and hurries toward what he desires. But you, what do you long for among the things you found when you entered the gate? For what do you give thanks? What great thing have you grasped? What have you found that was worth desiring? Explain your longing, so that Jewish shamelessness may never slander the truth. What did you find? What do you proclaim? What do you marvel at? "I found Christ," he says. "I saw the dispensation of Christ: the new grace, the strange kindness, the glorious passion, the ineffable initiation into the mystery. These things I see, these I marvel at, and giving thanks for them I say: I will give thanks to you, for you have heard me and have become my salvation. I do not hide this kindness or hoard this salvation. I proclaim the good news of the dispensation: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner." Do you see how the thanksgiving laid the story bare? "I will give thanks to you, for you have heard me and have become my salvation. The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner." Do you see how all the expectation of the prophets looked toward this very dispensation? It longed for Christ, who was despised in the synagogue but glorified among the nations. So, to return to our subject: even if you look for the gate, you will find Christ. "Yes," he says, "a door, out of love for mankind." But whoever enters the kingdom and temple of God must certainly have someone to lead him toward what he desires. No one dares to stand at the altar on his own without someone to act as priest. When you come inside the gate, do you find him as a priest who brings you near? "You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek." But a priest needs an offering and a victim to make God merciful. Again he himself becomes this for you: "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world." You have heard all these things that are for your sake. Now hear the things that belong to him in his own right. Do not stop your contemplation at the rank of priest. Do not see him standing as a priest. See him seated with the Father because of his own dignity. And let no one be an enemy of the truth, seizing on some things and hiding others. I know that some heretic, an enemy of the truth, has often stood up and said: "Do you see that it is impossible to approach the Father without the Son? He holds the rank of a mediator and a servant, bringing those who are saved to the Father." For since, the heretic says (new wisdom makes the truth new!), human nature was not able to approach God by itself, the Son becomes a borderland between created and uncreated nature, bringing the world near. Oh, this new madness! Oh, this new play on the stage! Among the heretics, the Father's overflowing goodness is put at risk, and the dignity of the Godhead is dulled. But though heretical madness grows bold, the Savior's power is not dulled, his glory is not quenched, and his grace is not torn down. "If we deny him," it says, "he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself." He sits with the Father because of his own dignity, and he stands as priest because of the love for mankind that befits him.

Now see something remarkable, brother. The heretics take the saying "No one comes to the Father except through me" in the sense of a servant's rank, as if he stood in the posture of one who waits on others. So we must turn the refutation of their impiety against them. If the Son's bringing people to the Father lowers the dignity of the one who brings them, what happens when you see the Father bringing people to the Son? Will you extend your impiety there too? In fact, by being impious toward the Son you blaspheme the Father most of all. So then, brothers, we who stand in the word of piety and truth must silence wickedness and make known the pious doctrine. "For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword." He calls the sword two-edged because its word works in two ways: one edge supports and the other strikes down. It strikes down the opponents of the faith and supports those who belong to it. Hear the Lord himself saying: "No one can come to me unless my heavenly Father draws him." We must say to the heretics what the case requires, brothers, and give the children of the faith full assurance about this idea. Why did the only-begotten Word of God divide this bringing near? In one place he says that people are brought to the Father by him, and in another that they are brought by the Father to him. The things of the divine nature are not confused. The word of truth is clear and well defined, with nothing crooked and nothing tangled in it: "For all the ways of the Lord are straight."

Does the Father, then, brothers, sometimes sit as king presiding and receive those who are brought to him, and at other times pay what is due to the Son, who sits enthroned in royal state, and stand by in a servant's rank to bring people to the Son? Far from it! When we speak of God sitting, we must not think of anything human. And again, when we hear of him standing, we must not think of anything belonging to our condition. If you hear that God stands, understand that the divine essence is unbending and upright. And if you read or hear that he sits, take it to mean that the blessed nature is steadfast and immovable. He himself says that he stands and that he sits. To Moses he says: "Stand here with me." And: "The place where the God of Israel stood was like a sapphire stone." Pay close attention. Moses speaks of him as standing, and God speaks to Moses as one who stands: "Stand with me." Then what do we make of Jeremiah's words: "You sit forever, and we perish forever"? Sitting and standing are human words, but their meanings are divine. Human life is unstable and is driven this way and that, so God is said to stand. Our condition is unsteady and turns in every direction, so he is said to sit, because of his steadfastness. Avoid what the bare wording suggests, and understand what faith contemplates. How, then, does the Son bring people to the Father, and how does the Father bring them to the Son? We must not leave the matter unexamined. The Father brings certain people to the Son, people we can identify and all agree on. The Son in turn brings certain people to the Father, again people we can identify and all agree on. Do not jump ahead and seize on this statement in order to slander it. Wait for the end, and then judge what is said. Do not be a hostile judge, but a friendly fellow contender. In Israel, God the Father was known, but the Son was unknown. Among the nations, both the Father and the Son were unknown, for the nations had been enslaved to the error of many gods. Where, then, the Father is known but the Son is not, the Father becomes the interpreter of the unknown Son. I will repeat the statement to fix the idea. Where the Father is known and the Son is doubted, the one who is known becomes the interpreter of the one who is unknown. Where the Father is unknown, the Son becomes the herald of the one who is unknown. So that you can examine what has been said precisely, I offer you the Gospel as guarantor. The Savior says about the nations: "I have made your name known to the world." Or rather, he means: to the world, which did not know it, I have made your name known. What name did he make known? That he is God? But knowledge had already reached that name. Even those in error speak of God, and those cut off from piety do not deny the title. What name, then, did he make known? That he is called Father. "I have made your name known to the world." Do you see that where the Father was unknown, the Son becomes the interpreter, making the truth clear by the proclamation of the gospel? But where the Father was thought to be known and the Son was not known, the Father himself becomes the interpreter of the one who was unknown. Let me show the truth from actual cases. Paul knew God, but did not know the Son. He knew God, but did not know that God was the Father of Christ. He was a zealot for piety, fighting for the law. God looked at his zeal, which was full of ignorance but brimming with longing. And what does he do? He makes the unknown one known to the man who did not know him. Who makes this clear to us? The very man who once did not know and later came to know, who once persecuted and later preached the gospel. What does he say? "I was a zealot for the law of my fathers, persecuting the church of God beyond measure. But when God, who set me apart from my mother's womb and called me through his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son in me..." and so on. A testimony is quoted to show the point at issue, not to explore its whole meaning. Again, the Savior asks the apostles: "Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?" He asks not in order to learn, but to banish conjecture and establish the truth. "Who do people say that I am?" First the apostles set out what the many suppose: "Some say Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets." What does the Savior do then? He gives no answer to the false opinions, judging these false conjectures unworthy of a reply. "But who do you say that I am? I am not concerned with the many who have gone astray, but with you who are to preach. You are the ones who will spread the lamp of truth and carry the proclamation of piety to all under heaven. The fate of mankind rests with you; the cause of truth is at stake in you. Just as your knowledge is a benefit shared by all people, so your ignorance would be a loss shared by the whole world. So: who do you say that I am?" Then Peter answered and said: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." This is the rule of faith, this is the word of truth, this is the confession of right belief. But this statement too might have been put on the same level as the others. So he, who had not thought the others worth an answer, gives his verdict on this one. And what does he say? He did not want this statement to be thought to come from human conjecture as well. So he sealed it and set the stamp of truth on it, saying: "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona." Here remember that the Father reveals the unknown one even to a man who knows the Father. "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven." Do you see that for the whole world, which did not know the Father, the Son becomes the interpreter of the one who was unknown? But for the synagogue and the Jews, who thought they knew God but did not recognize God the Word of God, the Father himself becomes the interpreter of the one who was in doubt.

So do not turn his surpassing love for humankind into provisions for impiety, and do not lessen his dignity because of the dispensation. Do not pry into a nature that cannot be measured; do not search out an essence that cannot be comprehended. Let Isaiah persuade you not to probe such things or write treatises about them: “Who will declare his generation?” But oh, the shameless audacity of those who dare to think and say everything so lightly! The Anomoean is not afraid as he searches into the nature of God, daring to speak what cannot be spoken and to make public what is holy. And no wonder. Since he does not know the truth, he professes to know what is unknown, so that he may hide what is proclaimed. He has not heard holy Scripture urging, “Reflect on what you have been commanded, for you have no need of hidden things.” The blessed God, the only Sovereign of wonders, once wished to astound Job, who shone out for his endurance, with the account of creation, and he says to him: “Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? … when the sea came to be” (to be brief) “when the mountains were formed? Did you keep watch over the birth of the goat-stags?” “Tell me,” he says, “how the world was ordered, the travail of the wild beasts and the feeding of the cattle, the constitution of everything in the world, its variety.” He said these things to him in order to teach him that even what appears in creation itself is beyond human comprehension. Then the blessed man, astounded, says: “Lord, I have spoken once, but a second time I will add nothing.” So the investigation of visible things defeated Job, and has not even the ineffable generation of the Only-begotten defeated your audacity? But since you announce what you do not know, I demand an account of what we all know. Tell me how the earth was established upon the waters. Tell me how Adam was formed from the earth. Tell me how the manna was supplied, how the sea was divided, and the rest of the wonders. Not to go on too long, tell me how the angels ate the calf that Abraham set before them. They had no stomach; the nature of angels had no receptacles for food. For “he makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flaming fire.” How was it consumed? At once the heretic says: “Why are you asking about something impossible? It vanished by the power of the angels.” So you believe in the power of angels and do not examine it, yet you pry into the generation of God? How did God make heaven and earth? He answers: “As he knows, as he willed.” So then the power of God is not subjected to reasonings but is entrusted to faith, while the divine generation is hemmed in by the constraints of reasoning? Have you not heard David saying, “Whatever the Lord willed, he has done”? You do not pry into his will, and yet you meddle with his nature? And what follows, brothers? What God made by willing is seen, but the one he begot from his own essence is invisible. For the visible works are an image of the invisible God. Is the invisible generation now to be made a slave to reasonings? What he made by an act of will is not scrutinized, and do you pry into what he brought forth according to his divine and undefiled nature? Oh, novel audacity! Oh, strange undertaking! Oh, the will honored and the nature insulted! Well did blessed David say: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek after falsehood?” For everything foreign to Christ’s teaching is both falsehood and vanity. For if he speaks the truth when he says, “I am the truth,” whatever lies outside Christ’s teaching leads to falsehood. Lift your soul up from questions that lie on the ground and from vain reasonings to the height of theology, and leave behind the poverty of inquiry by reasoning. Take hold of the treasure of truth. “The kingdom of heaven is like a hidden treasure.” Why is the Savior called a treasure? Here pay close attention. A treasure does not come into being at the moment it is found; it is old in its depositing and new in its finding. In the same way the saving Word is old in dignity and is the beginning of all things, since “In the beginning was the Word,” but the proclamation is new because of the dispensation of the flesh. Indeed, brother, so that you may learn that he shines out like a treasure to those who long for him, and that those who find him run to him as to a treasure discovered: Andrew, announcing the discovery to Peter, says, “We have found him of whom Moses wrote in the law, and the prophets also: the Christ.” For Moses and the prophets laid up the proclamation in the holy books as in treasuries. But just as people who store away a hidden treasure see for themselves what they lay down yet cover it from view, so that it may not become easy plunder for strangers, so too the prophets, when they proclaimed Christ, hid the treasure in the obscurity of their words. Why? Because if they had spoken plainly, it would not have been prophecy but proclamation, and the untimely declaration would have forestalled the proper time for the proclamation. What then do they do? They both interpret and conceal. Who says this? Isaiah: “And this book will be like a sealed book. If it is given to a man who knows letters, he will say, ‘I cannot read it, for it is sealed.’ And if it is given to one who does not know letters, he will say, ‘I cannot read it, for I have not learned letters.’” What then does this riddle mean? The prophecy about Christ, he is saying, was unknown both to Jews and to Greeks. It was unknown to the Jews, who knew letters, the law and the prophets, because it was sealed. The Jews knew letters and had been instructed. That is why God says to them: “You who have been carried from the womb and instructed until old age.” They were instructed, yet they did not know, since it was hidden by obscurity. To the Greeks it was unknown not because of obscurity, but because they did not know the letters at all. That is why Paul says to Timothy, who had been brought up in the law: “From infancy you have known the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation.” So the prophecy was stored up like treasure and hidden away in the holy books. For one must not turn away from what is hidden. And not only Isaiah shows that the prophecies were sealed, but Daniel too. For after disclosing to him the revelation of things to come, the angel says to him: “And you, Daniel, seal up this book of the vision, for its disclosure is far off.” That is why blessed David, reading the law and the prophets in the person of the people (for he who prophesied was not himself ignorant), and wishing to show that the people receive some glimpse of Christ’s dispensation but cannot understand it because of the obscurity of the words, felt something like people looking at a sealed purse. What then does he do, seeing the letters but not grasping their meaning? He says: “Unveil my eyes, and I will perceive the wonders of your law.” And again the same man: “Blessed are you, O Lord; teach me your statutes.” Did you not read them in the law? Did Moses not teach you the Ten Commandments? “But I want to learn what is yours, from you, the Lawgiver; I want to learn the truth of the law from the source of the law.” He sought to learn, but the grace was being kept in store for those who were to receive the benefit. That is why the Savior said to the disciples: “Many kings and righteous men longed to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it; but blessed are your eyes, because they see.”

But we are asking when the seal was finally broken, when the bond of ignorance was loosed, when what had been shut was opened. The listener demands it of us: “In the course of your sermon,” he says, “you have explained to me how the sealing was done; will you not tell me when the sealed things were released? You have shown me the gates shut; will you not show me them opened?” What then? I will set aside many things and present what is being asked from a single saying. What then? After the Savior’s resurrection, while divine grace was still unknown to most, two of the disciples, it says, were going out to a village, and as friends will on a journey, they were discussing the dispensation with each other. The Savior changed his appearance and his voice (for what the face is to those who see, the voice is to those who cannot see the face). He hid both voice and form, and he who knows all things says to them: “What are these words that you are exchanging with each other?” The one who learns everything from him says to him who knows everything: “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there?” He says: “What things?” This God who knows all things and yet asks is the Son of the one who said to Cain, “Where is Abel your brother?” They say: “The things about Jesus of Nazareth, who was a man mighty in word and deed.” Still a man? After so many miracles, a man? After such mighty works, after such a display of divine power? “But we,” it says (I will not examine every detail, or the sermon will grow too long), “but we had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel.” See how faith had almost been extinguished in them, and the hope of the dispensation had by now been demolished. “We were expecting.” He does not say “we expect,” but “we were expecting.” He knew, then, that their faith had grown weak and their minds had sunk. And there came to them the one who upholds those who have fallen and raises up all who are cast down. And what does the Benefactor say to them? “O foolish and slow of heart, do you not understand the Scriptures? Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and to enter into his glory?” And beginning from the law and the prophets, he opened the Scriptures to them. You see that until Christ came to them, the gate of truth was not opened, nor was the bond of ignorance loosed. He opened the Scriptures like doors that had been shut. What doors? Those Paul speaks of: “that God may open a door to the Gentiles.” And again, concerning Cornelius: “So God has opened to the Gentiles too the door of repentance?” And see what the Fountain of good things arranges. When he came to the village of Emmaus, where the travelers were heading, he was still unrecognized by them, and he appeared to them while they were in doubt. For when he reclined at table with them, at first being shown hospitality as a stranger (“Stay with us,” they say, “for the day is far spent”), then, so that ignorance might not wholly veil his dignity, he took bread, blessed it, broke it and gave it to them, and their eyes were opened and they recognized him. Why did he first give the bread, and only then were their eyes opened? Since Adam’s eating opened his eyes to harm, an eating was now brought in its place that works a wondrous recovery of sight. Let the children of the heretics also recover their sight and see the light of truth. Let them see the God who was in the beginning, who is God and is the Word of God. Let them hear “was” again and again, and stop saying “he was not.” “In the beginning was the Word.” This was not proclaimed at once, for the world could not take it in. There are, of course, four evangelists: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. When they began their proclamation, they did not at once speak what befits his dignity, but what suited their hearers. Matthew, opening the Gospels, says: “The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.” Why not “Son of God”? Why do you hide his dignity in so poor a phrase? Why do you veil divine things from human beings? “I am preaching among Jews,” he says, “who do not even believe that Christ was a righteous man. They have not yet accepted him as son of Abraham, and will they put up with hearing him proclaimed Son of God?” And how do we know this? Because they did not even acknowledge that he was of Abraham’s race. Have you not heard how often they blasphemed him, saying, “You are a Samaritan and have a demon”? Would those who cast him out of the race of the saints grasp his divine dignity? What then does he say? “The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.” First he draws them in with familiar names, names bound to them by kinship, so that, caught by these, they might little by little find the truth: the generation that is without passion and undefiled, proclaimed in language worthy of God and handed down to all. Next blessed Mark, launching into the Gospel and emboldened by those who had already been prepared, does say “Son of God,” but at once he drew in his words and cut the thought short, in order to soften the hearer. So he immediately brings in the account of the Baptist, saying: “The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ. As it is written in Isaiah the prophet: ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’” He showed the torch of truth and at once hid it again. He puts forward the servant first, so that the hearer, led along by that voice, might afterward receive soundly the complete word of the knowledge of God. Luke follows third and walks in the middle between them. He touches on the divine Word but does not explain or unfold his dignity. Instead he says: “Since many have undertaken to compile a narrative of the things that have been fulfilled among us, it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely from the beginning, to write, just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the Word handed them down to us.” He said “Word,” but he did not say that the Word was also God. What then does he too do? He touches on the Word’s being, but realizing that he was sounding in dead ears, he hides the dignity and puts forward the dispensation: “There was a priest named Zechariah,” and the rest of the Gospel. All of them, then, went on to the dispensation of the flesh, and gently, in a way, made his dignity known through the miracles. The rank of God the Word was proclaimed, but the arrows against the heretics were kept hidden, and the bulwark of right doctrine had not yet been raised by the proclamation of true religion. John, then, the son of thunder, came last to theology, after those three heralds. And fittingly he followed while they went ahead, flashing the lesser things in the meantime. For just as lightning goes before thunder, so that thunder bursting suddenly from the clouds may not strike the hearer, so too, since John was going to thunder, the three evangelists went first like lightnings: they flashed out the dispensation, and he thunders out the theology. Thunder, brothers, comes with rain; thunder is a terror to the wicked. Heaven summons the rain, using the thunder as a kind of trumpet, but first it calls forth the shower with lightnings (for “God made lightnings for the rain”), and then it stirs the clouds with thunder. What then? Since so many lightnings of the Word went before, there follows next, as I said earlier, the thunder of theology. It astonishes many by the surpassing greatness of its theology, but it brings showers of blessing. For us it becomes the thunder of theology, but for the heretics it is a thunder that drives off the evil beasts by the overwhelming power of its voice. “At your rebuke they will flee; at the sound of your thunder they will be afraid.”

Let us run back, then, to the God who was in the beginning; let us run back to the eternal light; let us run back to the Word who became man for your sake. When I say “became,” I do not mean a nature that was changed, but the divine dignity taking up what is ours. For “the Word became flesh” does not indicate an alteration of nature, but the assumption of our weakness. If you think “became” means change, then when you hear Paul saying, “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us,” you will take the phrase to mean that he changed into a curse by nature. Just as “having become a curse” means nothing other than that he took upon himself the curse that lay on us, so too “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” indicates nothing other than the assumption of the flesh. You have an image within yourself. Your own word will teach you about God the Word, not because it bears a complete likeness, but because it is a trace and reflection of the divine dignity. Here pay close attention, so that the words are not spoken in vain and the divine meanings lost. The human word (the image is faint and does not present the whole dignity, but teaches what is beyond us from what is ours), our word, is incorporeal, invisible, intangible, conveyed by hearing alone. No one knows a word by sight; no one has held one in his hand. It is invisible and intangible, grasped by one sense only, hearing, and even that invisibly. For hearing does not stretch out hands to take hold of it; rather the word itself enters and is held. The word is an offspring of the mind; but it is begotten not through passion, not through sight [?], not through division. It is not parted from the mind that begot it, not separated, not split off. Here lend me your ear, heretic: first understand what is your own, and then form an idea of what is above you. The mind begets, the word goes forth; it goes forth from its begetter and fills all who hear it, and yet it does not depart from the one that begot it. The word goes forth, distributed to everyone and nowhere divided. For each person receives the whole word, and it is in each; though distributed among so many, it is poured in whole. So our word shows in itself the mind that begot it, for the thought is grasped from the word. Consider this too. In sketching beforehand the dispensation of God the Word through this word of ours, God has drawn in advance a marvelous image, adorned with earthly flowers yet fitting for a preliminary contemplation of the Word. What is it? Our word is invisible, has no body and cannot be held; but God, by a further kind of wisdom, has refashioned it and made it visible and able to be held. What does he do? Since it could not be seen by the eye, he clothes it with writing as with a body, and has put around it the visible form of the letters as a kind of flesh. The word that you once heard but did not see, you now see when you read; the word you could not meet, you carry about in a book. But though the word takes a body through writing, it is not enclosed by the writing; it remains with the speaker and with the reader. And if someone, brothers, takes a book and tears it up, he has torn the body of the word, but he has not cut the word. So that you may learn that the word is not destroyed along with the writing, God says to Jeremiah: “Sit down and write in a book all the words, and give it to King Jehoiakim.” The word was full of reproof. Since rulers cannot bear reproofs (for high rank does not easily submit to what is just, but blunts the truth), the king, stung by the reproofs, tears the book apart, cuts it up with the scribe’s knife and took it, it says, to the fire in the brazier. What then does God say to Jeremiah? “Sit down and write the same words and give them to the king,” so that he might learn that he had cut up the writing but had not severed the word. Do you see the image? Now raise your mind to the heights. The Word of God, himself God, the Only-begotten, puts on a body, so that he who is not seen may appear; he puts on flesh, so that he who cannot be held may be held. That is why John, having found that object of his longing, once grasped by hearing but later held by sight, says: “That which was from the beginning, which we have seen and heard, and which our hands have touched.” He wore the flesh, then, as a garment of his dignity, a comely garment: “For the Lord reigns; he has clothed himself with majesty.” The Jews fight against what is seen, not knowing what is unseen; they crucify the flesh, but they do not destroy the Godhead. If my word does not vanish along with the writing, which is the garment of the word, did God the Word, the fountain of life, die along with the flesh? The suffering belongs to the body; the freedom from suffering belongs to the dignity. Why then does Paul say, “For if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory”? Because he who put on the flesh makes the suffering of the flesh his own. If you insult a royal robe, do you not insult the one who wears it? Do you not know that if someone insults the king’s image, he carries the insult to the original whose dignity it bears? Do you not know that if someone pulls down an image of wood or a bronze statue, he is not judged as having dared something against lifeless matter, but is put to death as one who stretched out his hands against the king? Lifeless matter bearing the king’s image refers the insult done to it to the king; and did not the living form that God the Word put on, when it was insulted, refer the insult to the one who put it on? Understand, then, the dignity, and do not insult the dispensation. But this is enough. Let us save what remains of the contemplation of God the Word for another sermon, and so respect due proportion by keeping order, and let us send up glory to God, to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
